content: Scientists have used radio waves to control the magnetic spin of a single atomic nucleus, achieving a result that challenges their understanding of how atomic magnetism works. The experiment, conducted at Delft University of Technology and published in Nature Communications , demonstrates that nuclear spin can be manipulated under conditions where researchers did not expect it to respond. Unlike the relatively strong magnetism associated with electrons, nuclear magnetism is extremely weak and more isolated from its surroundings. “By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons,” says lead researcher Sander Otte. “But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world.” To investigate magnetism at the atomic scale, Otte’s team uses a modified scanning tunneling microscope capable of directing electrical signals at individual atoms. Previous experiments primarily examined electron spin, which is easier to detect and manipulate. Nuclear spin could be observed indirectly through the hyperfine interaction, a quantum coupling between the magnetic properties of an electron and the nucleus. In the latest experiment, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues applied two signals simultaneously, one targeting the electron and another targeting the nucleus. By examining their effects separately, the researchers discovered that they could flip the nuclear spin even when it was largely disentangled from the electron spin. This contradicted their expectation that the nucleus would not respond independently to the microscope’s electrical signals. “According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen,” says Otte. “The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope.” The researchers achieved this control by adapting double magnetic resonance, an established technique, to work with a single atom. The method allowed them to address the nucleus and electron independently using signals tuned to their respective magnetic resonances. In quantum mechanics, spin can change between specific allowed states, and each transition requires a signal with the appropriate frequency. “You can compare it to the strings of a guitar,” Vennema explains. “Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The ‘notes’ of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin.” Nuclear spins are promising candidates for storing quantum information because they are relatively well protected from external disturbances that can disrupt delicate quantum states. The ability to control an individual nuclear spin could eventually support new methods for storing and reading quantum information, although practical applications remain a future possibility. For now, the experiment leaves a fundamental question unanswered: What physical mechanism allows the nuclear spin to respond when its coupling to the electron spin is insufficient to explain the observed behavior? Understanding that process will require further investigation. “Back to the drawing board, then,” says Otte. “That is really how science works. There is always something new left to figure out.” Reference: “Nuclear magnetic resonance on a single atom with a local probe” by Hester G. Vennema, Cristina Mier, Evert W. Stolte, Leonard Edens, Jinwon Lee and Sander Otte, 24 October 2026, Nature Communications . DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78801-5 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. title: SoftBank swings to $7 billion loss after U.S. data center hit and Intel share decline
content: SoftBank reported a fiscal second-quarter net loss of 1.12 trillion yen ($7 billion) on Tuesday, as losses tied to U.S. AI data center equipment procurement and Intel share declines weighed on earnings. The Japanese investment giant also recorded a 597.2 billion ($3.7 billion) yen loss in the six months ending on Sept. 30 due to changes in procurement plans for power generation equipment for AI data center projects in the U.S. SoftBank said it had made advance investments to secure power generation equipment for its AI data center projects in the U.S. amid concerns over potential shortages and long procurement lead times. Power is increasingly becoming a key constraint for the AI data center buildout as power grids become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers. Cumulative payments for power-generation equipment for U.S. AI data center projects, like the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County, Ohio, totaled $9.48 billion as of the end of September. "We made bridge investments in advance to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortage," a SoftBank executive said during the company's earnings call. Here's how SoftBank fared in the fiscal second quarter: Revenue rose 13.3% in the six months ended Sept. 30, supported by growth in telecommunications and AI computing businesses. The company said its SoftBank segment recorded higher sales across all businesses, while revenue at its AI computing segment increased. The company's Vision Fund segment swung to a loss of 81.58 billion yen in the fiscal second quarter, compared with a profit of 2.38 trillion yen a year earlier. Vision Fund 1 recorded an investment loss of $20 million in the quarter, despite a $1.3 billion gain on ByteDance, as shares of publicly traded portfolio companies, including Coupang and Grab, declined. The Vision Funds segment recorded investment gains of 85.45 billion yen, down sharply from 2.81 trillion yen in the year-earlier period. Vision Fund 2 posted investment gains of 89.26 billion yen, while Vision Fund 1 recorded a loss of 3.86 billion yen on its investments. As of the end of September, SoftBank's cumulative investment in OpenAI stood at $54.6 billion, with a fair value of $99.6 billion and a cumulative investment gain of $45 billion, according to the company. SoftBank said a potential increase in OpenAI's valuation following a new funding round had not yet been reflected in its results, pending an official announcement. The updated valuation could be reflected in the fiscal third quarter, potentially boosting its net asset value and improving its loan-to-value ratio, the company said. "ChatGPT has been continuously a weapon of OpenAI, especially for consumers," the SoftBank esecutive said during the company's earnings call, highlighting the chatbot's growing user base. Shares of the Japanese investment giant closed 13.9% higher on Tuesday. The gains came as Asian technology stocks, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, rose following an overnight rebound on Wall Street. On its AI infrastructure investments, SoftBank highlighted a 20-year lease agreement with OpenAI for eight gigawatts of IT capacity at a data center project in Ohio. Addressing concerns of water consumption at its planned data center in Texas, SoftBank said it was taking steps to reduce water use through a closed-loop, air-cooled system. The company also pointed to plans to hire and source locally. Ahead of its earnings release, SoftBank Group announced on Monday plans with Grab and Malaysia's PETROS to commit a combined $1.85 billion in initial capital to develop AI infrastructure in Malaysia, with a long-term target of at least five gigawatts of AI computing capacity.

analysis.reason: The article reports a significant development in the technology sector, specifically in the area of AI data center projects.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant development in the technology sector, specifically in the area of AI data center projects, with a $7 billion loss for SoftBank, providing a clear reason for readers to care about the implications of power generation equipment procurement for AI data center buildout.

title: Galileo spent his life proving Earth wasn’t center stage. Now his story is heading to Broadway
content: Galileo Galilei is among the most recognizable rebels of the late Renaissance. Now, a new Broadway musical puts a rock-and-roll spin on the radical life of the “Father of Modern Science,” whose ideas clashed with the powerful Roman Catholic Church and helped propel the Scientific Revolution. “Galileo,” starring Raúl Esparza and Joy Woods, follows the famed astronomer as his research on the heliocentric model challenged prevailing Aristotelian wisdom that the Earth sat at the center of the cosmos. The show is set to begin preview performances November 10 at New York City’s Shubert Theatre before opening December 6. Director Michael Mayer, who has worked on the production for nearly a decade, knew instinctively that Galileo, born in 1564 Italy, had the energy of a modern-day rock star: Historians have described him as defiant as well as arrogant and subversive. “I said, ‘I think this should be a rock musical,’” Mayer said. “He literally rocked our world.” Astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson, who serves as a coproducer for the musical, more bluntly describes Galileo as “a bit of an a**hole.” But his egotism, perhaps more than his research alone, ultimately led to his fall from favor with church authorities, who banned his writings for more than 200 years and relegated him to house arrest in Tuscany, said Tyson, who is the director of the Hayden Planetarium at the American Museum of Natural History in New York. “Had he been more politic about it,” Tyson said, “he might not have met the fate that he did.” He died in confinement in 1642, but Galileo’s ideas endured and spread. Two centuries after his death, the Catholic Church lifted its ban on his works as it became irrefutably evident that the combative astronomer had been right all along. Tyson, Mayer and Esparza said they hope that bringing Galileo’s story to Broadway will prove particularly prescient in today’s political climate. “It is a man who is standing up for what is objectively true against dogmatic forces that would suppress those truths,” Tyson said. “This is something that we need in these times.” From his home in the city of Padua in northern Italy, under the shadow of a Catholic Church increasingly concerned with enforcing orthodoxy, Galileo became one of the most adept users of the newly invented telescope. Based on his observations with a homemade telescope, in 1610, he became the first to suggest that Jupiter had moons. After observing how light moved across Venus’ surface, Galileo became even more zealous in his belief that Renaissance astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus had been correct when he hypothesized in the early 1500s that the planets, including Earth, revolve around the sun. But as Galileo began to share his findings, he drew the attention of Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, sometimes called the “Hammer of Heretics.” The cardinal made it clear to Galileo that a heliocentric model contradicted scripture and ordered him to abandon the topic. Bellarmine is absent from the Broadway show, which introduces a few fictionalized church leaders. A lovelorn portrayal of one of Galileo’s daughters, Virginia — played by Woods — also takes some creative liberties. While her character is a bright scientist who plays an active role in Galileo’s research, the real-life daughter of the astronomer was living in a convent by age 13 , where she developed expertise as an apothecary . But the production also draws heavily on real events, including experiments that Galileo carried out as he began to question nearly 2,000 years of accepted wisdom about the laws of motion. Using an incline plane, for example, Galileo demonstrated that objects accelerate as they fall. Years later, after Galileo’s first confrontation with the Roman Inquisition barred him from spreading Copernican theory, he found a powerful ally in Pope Urban VIII — portrayed by Jeremy Kushnier in the musical. Believing he had the pope’s support, he published one of his most famous works: “Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems.” He wrote the text in Italian rather than Latin so his ideas could be read by the masses. The text was supposed to be a presentation of the arguments for and against a sun-centric model, but Galileo once again drew the church’s ire by including the character “Simplicio,” who parroted talking points used by the pope himself — leading to an abrupt rupture in his relationship with Urban VIII. “He cannot help himself,” said Esparza, who is making a highly anticipated return to Broadway after 14 years. “I think he thinks he’s smarter than everybody in the room.” Facing the Roman Inquisition in 1633, Galileo was accused of heresy, a charge that had led others to be burned alive. He renounced his positions on heliocentrism. To bring the story to life, Esparza noted that the production team brought on Ethan Tobman, the creative director for Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour, to design stunning effects that transform the Shubert Theatre into an immersive digital starfield, reminiscent of a planetarium. “It’s almost vertigo-inducing, and I love that because if you’re doing a show about technology, you want the audience to experience something they’ve never seen before,” Esparza said. The business of Broadway is notoriously fickle, and figuring out which magic combination of subject matter and musical style will resonate with an audience can be a daunting undertaking. But Galileo’s life is rife with lessons about curiosity, sacrifice and compromise that Mayer and Tyson hope will move audiences. His story is one of science history’s most famous tales, Tyson said. “How come this hasn’t been a musical? How come no one did this decades ago?”
ranking_reason: Galileo's life and research are being brought to Broadway, highlighting his contributions to the Scientific Revolution.

analysis.reason: Galileo's life and research are being brought to Broadway, highlighting his contributions to the Scientific Revolution.

final_quality.reason: The article reports on the cultural significance of a Broadway musical that brings Galileo's story to life, highlighting his contributions to the Scientific Revolution. The inclusion of quotes from experts like Neil deGrasse Tyson adds depth to the story, making it a substantive and important development in the science and technology category.
